units.title: Scarcity and Choice
units.blurb: Why every choice has a cost, how economists separate facts from values, and how societies decide what to make and who gets it.

units.title: Production Possibilities and Trade
units.blurb: The production possibilities curve, opportunity cost in production, growth, and why specializing and trading can make both sides better off.

units.title: Thinking at the Margin
units.blurb: Decide one unit at a time: compare marginal benefit with marginal cost, ignore sunk costs, and spend where the next dollar does the most good.

units.title: Supply and Demand
units.blurb: Demand and supply schedules, what shifts each curve, market equilibrium, and how prices and quantities respond to change.

units.title: Elasticity
units.blurb: How strongly quantities respond to price and income, what makes demand elastic, and what elasticity means for a seller's revenue.

units.title: Efficiency and Government in Markets
units.blurb: Consumer and producer surplus, deadweight loss, and what price controls, taxes, subsidies and trade barriers do to a market.

units.title: Production and Costs
units.blurb: Economic profit, the short-run production function, cost curves and how they relate, and economies of scale in the long run.

units.title: Perfect Competition
units.blurb: Price-taking firms, the MR = MC rule, profit and loss, when to shut down, and long-run equilibrium with entry and exit.

units.title: Imperfect Competition
units.blurb: Monopoly, natural monopoly and its regulation, price discrimination, monopolistic competition, and oligopolies as strategic games.

units.title: Factor Markets
units.blurb: Derived demand for labor, the hiring rule MRP = MRC, shifts in labor markets, the least-cost mix of inputs, and monopsony.

units.title: Market Failure and the Role of Government
units.blurb: Externalities, public goods and common resources, the policies that address them, and how income inequality is measured.

topics.title: Scarcity and the Factors of Production
topics.short: Wants outrun resources, so land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship must be rationed somehow.
topics.trouble: Students treat money as capital and think scarcity means a shortage or poverty. In economics, capital means tools, machines and buildings, and even a rich society faces scarcity.

topics.title: Opportunity Cost
topics.short: The cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative you give up, including your time.
topics.trouble: Students add up every alternative instead of taking only the best one, and leave out costs that are not paid in money, such as time or a wage given up.

topics.title: Positive and Normative Statements
topics.short: A positive statement can be checked against facts; a normative statement says what ought to be.
topics.trouble: Students call a statement normative because they disagree with it, or positive because it sounds scientific. A positive claim can be false and still be positive.

topics.title: Economic Systems
topics.short: Markets, command and tradition each answer what to make, how to make it and who gets it; real economies mix them.
topics.trouble: Students picture a real country as a pure market or pure command economy. Every modern economy is mixed; countries differ in the balance.

topics.title: Budget Constraints
topics.short: A budget line shows every affordable combination of two goods, and its slope is an opportunity cost.
topics.trouble: Students put the wrong intercept on each axis (income divided by the other good's price) or read the slope's ratio upside down.

topics.title: The Production Possibilities Curve
topics.short: Points on the curve are efficient, points inside waste resources, and points outside cannot be produced yet.
topics.trouble: Students call a point inside the curve impossible, or think the curve shows what people want rather than what can be produced.

topics.title: Opportunity Cost Along the PPC
topics.short: A straight PPC means constant opportunity cost; a bowed-out PPC means the cost rises as you make more.
topics.trouble: Students report the amount gained instead of the amount given up, or flip the ratio (2 cars per computer instead of 1/2 computer per car).

topics.title: Growth and Shifts of the PPC
topics.short: More resources or better technology push the curve out; idle resources put the economy at a point inside it.
topics.trouble: Students shift the whole curve out when idle workers go back to work. That moves a point from inside toward the curve; only new resources or technology shift it.

topics.title: Absolute and Comparative Advantage
topics.short: Comparative advantage goes to whoever gives up less of the other good, not to whoever makes more.
topics.trouble: Students confuse absolute with comparative advantage, and in input problems (hours per unit) they treat the bigger number as better.

topics.title: Specialization and the Terms of Trade
topics.short: Trade helps both sides when the price lies between the two producers' opportunity costs.
topics.trouble: Students think trade is a contest in which one side's gain is the other's loss, or that a country better at everything has nothing to gain from trade.

topics.title: Marginal Benefit, Marginal Cost and Sunk Costs
topics.short: Keep going while the next unit's benefit is at least its cost; money already spent should not change the choice.
topics.trouble: Students pick the quantity with the largest total benefit instead of the largest net benefit, and let sunk costs ("we already paid for the tickets") drive the decision.

topics.title: Total and Marginal Utility
topics.short: Each extra unit usually adds less satisfaction than the one before it.
topics.trouble: Students think total utility falls as soon as marginal utility falls. Total utility keeps rising as long as marginal utility is positive.

topics.title: Marginal Utility per Dollar
topics.short: Spend so the last dollar on each good adds the same utility: MUx/Px = MUy/Py.
topics.trouble: Students compare marginal utilities without dividing by price, so they buy more of whatever is most enjoyable no matter what it costs.

topics.title: The Law of Demand
topics.short: Other things equal, a higher price means a smaller quantity demanded.
topics.trouble: Students think "demand" means one number, the amount bought, rather than the whole relationship between price and quantity demanded.

topics.title: Demand Equations Both Ways
topics.short: Q = 20 − 2P and P = 10 − Q/2 describe the same demand curve, drawn with price on the vertical axis.
topics.trouble: Students who learned y = f(x) mix up the price intercept with the quantity intercept, or take the −2 in Q = 20 − 2P as the slope of the graph; with price on the vertical axis the slope is −1/2.

topics.title: Change in Demand vs Change in Quantity Demanded
topics.short: A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; any other change in buying plans shifts the whole curve.
topics.trouble: Students confuse a change in demand with a change in quantity demanded, for example saying "the price fell, so demand increased."

topics.title: What Shifts Demand
topics.short: Tastes, income, expectations and the number of buyers shift demand; more income raises demand for normal goods and lowers it for inferior goods.
topics.trouble: Students assume more income raises demand for every good. "Inferior" is an economic term for goods people buy less of as income rises, not a judgment of quality.

topics.title: Substitutes and Complements
topics.short: A higher price for coffee raises demand for tea (a substitute) and lowers demand for coffee filters (a complement).
topics.trouble: Students shift the demand curve of the good whose own price changed instead of the related good's curve, mixing a movement along one curve with a shift of another.

topics.title: The Law of Supply
topics.short: Other things equal, a higher price brings a larger quantity supplied, because extra units cost more to make.
topics.trouble: Students say a higher price "increases supply" (a shift) when it increases the quantity supplied (a movement along the curve).

topics.title: What Shifts Supply
topics.short: Input prices, technology, taxes and subsidies, expectations and the number of sellers shift supply.
topics.trouble: Students read the upward shift of supply after a cost increase as "more supply." A shift up and to the left is a decrease in supply.

topics.title: Market Equilibrium
topics.short: The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, found on a graph or by setting the two equations equal.
topics.trouble: Students solve Qd = Qs for the price and then report that number as the quantity, or plug the price into only one equation without checking the other.

topics.title: Shortages and Surpluses
topics.short: Below the equilibrium price there is a shortage, above it a surplus, and each pushes the price back toward equilibrium.
topics.trouble: Students confuse a shortage (quantity demanded above quantity supplied at the current price) with scarcity, or think a surplus pushes the price up.

topics.title: When One Curve Shifts
topics.short: Decide which curve shifts and which way, then read the new equilibrium price and quantity.
topics.trouble: Students "double shift": the price rises, so supply increases, so the price falls. The price change is a movement along the curve that did not shift, not a second shift.

topics.title: When Both Curves Shift
topics.short: With two shifts, either price or quantity changes in a definite direction and the other depends on which shift is larger.
topics.trouble: Students give a definite answer for the variable that is ambiguous instead of saying it depends on the sizes of the shifts.

topics.title: Price Elasticity of Demand
topics.short: Divide the percent change in quantity demanded by the percent change in price, using the midpoint method.
topics.trouble: Students divide in the wrong order (price over quantity), use the slope instead of percent changes, or use different bases for the two percent changes.

topics.title: Elastic, Inelastic and What Decides It
topics.short: Close substitutes, luxuries, a large share of the budget and more time to adjust all make demand more elastic.
topics.trouble: Students judge elasticity by how steep the graph looks. Slope and elasticity differ, and elasticity changes from point to point along a straight-line demand curve.

topics.title: Elasticity and Total Revenue
topics.short: A higher price raises revenue only when demand is inelastic; revenue is largest where demand is unit elastic.
topics.trouble: Students believe a price increase always raises revenue because each unit brings in more money.

topics.title: Price Elasticity of Supply
topics.short: Supply is more elastic when firms have time, spare capacity and easy access to inputs.
topics.trouble: Students give supply elasticity a minus sign out of habit, or think a perfectly inelastic supply curve is horizontal rather than vertical.

topics.title: Income and Cross-Price Elasticity
topics.short: The sign tells the story: normal or inferior goods for income elasticity, substitutes or complements for cross-price elasticity.
topics.trouble: Students drop the sign as they do for price elasticity, but for these two elasticities the sign carries the meaning.

topics.title: Consumer and Producer Surplus
topics.short: Buyers gain the gap between what they would pay and the price; sellers gain the gap between the price and their cost.
topics.trouble: Students confuse consumer surplus with total spending (price times quantity), or measure the triangle out to the wrong quantity.

topics.title: Total Surplus and Deadweight Loss
topics.short: A competitive market with no spillovers maximizes total surplus; trading too little or too much loses some of it.
topics.trouble: Students think the lost surplus is money that someone else collects. A deadweight loss is a gain from trade that no one gets.

topics.title: Price Ceilings and Price Floors
topics.short: A binding ceiling sits below equilibrium and causes a shortage; a binding floor sits above it and causes a surplus.
topics.trouble: Students place a binding ceiling above the equilibrium price because "ceiling" sounds high, and think a ceiling above equilibrium changes the market.

topics.title: Per-Unit Taxes
topics.short: A tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep, raising revenue and causing a deadweight loss.
topics.trouble: Students expect the market price to rise by the full amount of the tax, or compute tax revenue with the quantity from before the tax.

topics.title: Who Really Pays a Tax
topics.short: The less elastic side of the market bears more of a tax, no matter who sends the money to the government.
topics.trouble: Students think whoever is legally required to pay the tax also bears its burden.

topics.title: Per-Unit Subsidies
topics.short: A subsidy lowers the price buyers pay, raises the price sellers get, costs taxpayers money and leads to more than the efficient quantity.
topics.trouble: Students count the gains to buyers and sellers but forget the cost to taxpayers, so they conclude a subsidy must raise total surplus.

topics.title: Trade at the World Price
topics.short: When a country opens to trade, the world price decides whether it imports or exports, and who gains and who loses.
topics.trouble: Students see only the loss to domestic producers and conclude the country as a whole is worse off. In the model, consumers gain more than producers lose, though the losses are real and fall on particular people.

topics.title: Tariffs and Import Quotas
topics.short: A tariff or quota raises the domestic price, helps domestic producers, costs consumers more and creates deadweight loss.
topics.trouble: Students think foreign producers pay the tariff, or miss that a quota raises the price like a tariff but lets license holders, not the government, keep the extra money.

topics.title: Accounting and Economic Profit
topics.short: Economic profit subtracts implicit costs too, so zero economic profit is a normal return.
topics.trouble: Students leave out implicit costs such as the owner's forgone salary, and think zero economic profit means the business is failing.

topics.title: Short-Run Production
topics.short: Adding workers to a fixed plant eventually adds less output each time: diminishing marginal returns.
topics.trouble: Students confuse diminishing marginal returns (marginal product falling) with negative returns (total product falling), or with diseconomies of scale.

topics.title: Short-Run Costs
topics.short: Fixed, variable and total cost, and the average and marginal costs computed from them.
topics.trouble: Students compute marginal cost as total cost divided by quantity, or let fixed cost change with output.

topics.title: How Marginal and Average Costs Relate
topics.short: Marginal cost crosses average variable cost and average total cost at their lowest points.
topics.trouble: Students think marginal cost is at its lowest where it crosses average total cost. The crossing is at the lowest point of the average, not of marginal cost.

topics.title: What Shifts the Cost Curves
topics.short: A change in fixed cost, such as a license fee or lump-sum tax, moves only ATC and AFC; a change in variable cost moves MC, AVC and ATC.
topics.trouble: Students shift marginal cost when fixed cost changes, and so predict that a lump-sum fee changes how much a firm produces.

topics.title: Economies and Diseconomies of Scale
topics.short: In the long run every input can change; average cost may fall, stay flat, then rise as the firm grows.
topics.trouble: Students confuse diseconomies of scale (a long-run idea about the size of the whole firm) with diminishing marginal returns (a short-run idea about one input).

topics.title: Perfect Competition and Price Takers
topics.short: Many sellers of an identical product each face a flat demand curve at the market price, so P = MR.
topics.trouble: Students give the single firm a downward-sloping demand curve because the market demand curve slopes down.

topics.title: Profit-Maximizing Output: MR = MC
topics.short: Produce every unit whose marginal revenue covers its marginal cost, and stop where MR = MC.
topics.trouble: Students pick the output with the highest total revenue or the highest profit per unit instead of the output where MR = MC.

topics.title: Profit and Loss on the Graph
topics.short: Profit equals (P − ATC) × Q, a rectangle between the price and average total cost.
topics.trouble: Students measure profit per unit as price minus marginal cost instead of price minus average total cost.

topics.title: The Shutdown Rule
topics.short: In the short run, keep producing if price covers average variable cost, even at a loss.
topics.trouble: Students think a firm should shut down as soon as it makes a loss, forgetting that it pays its fixed costs either way in the short run.

topics.title: Entry, Exit and the Long Run
topics.short: Profits draw new firms in and losses push firms out until price equals minimum average total cost.
topics.trouble: Students treat zero economic profit as no reward for owners, and shift the firm's cost curves instead of the market supply curve when firms enter.

topics.title: Allocative and Productive Efficiency
topics.short: Allocative efficiency means P = MC; productive efficiency means producing at minimum ATC.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the two conditions, or think an efficient outcome must also be a fair one.

topics.title: Monopoly and Barriers to Entry
topics.short: Economies of scale, legal protection such as patents, control of a key resource and network effects can keep rivals out.
topics.trouble: Students think a monopoly can charge any price it likes. It still faces the downward-sloping market demand curve, so a higher price means fewer sales.

topics.title: Why Marginal Revenue Is Below Price
topics.short: To sell one more unit, a single-price seller must lower the price on every unit, so MR < P.
topics.trouble: Students set marginal revenue equal to price as in perfect competition, forgetting the revenue lost on the units that could have sold at the higher price.

topics.title: The Monopolist's Price and Output
topics.short: Find the quantity where MR = MC, then go up to the demand curve to read the price.
topics.trouble: Students read the price off the MC or MR curve at the MR = MC quantity instead of off the demand curve.

topics.title: Monopoly and Deadweight Loss
topics.short: A monopoly sells less at a higher price than a competitive market would, so P > MC and some surplus is lost.
topics.trouble: Students count the monopolist's extra profit as the deadweight loss. Most of it is surplus moved from consumers to the firm; the deadweight loss is the triangle no one gets.

topics.title: Regulating a Natural Monopoly
topics.short: When one firm can serve a market most cheaply, regulators may set P = MC (efficient but loss-making) or P = ATC (a fair return).
topics.trouble: Students expect a P = MC price rule to let the firm break even. With average cost falling, marginal cost is below average total cost, so the firm loses money.

topics.title: Price Discrimination
topics.short: Charging different buyers different prices for the same good can raise both output and profit while shrinking consumer surplus.
topics.trouble: Students call any price difference discrimination (costs may differ), and miss the conditions it needs: market power, a way to sort buyers, and no resale.

topics.title: Monopolistic Competition
topics.short: Many firms with differentiated products earn zero economic profit in the long run and have excess capacity.
topics.trouble: Students expect long-run profits as in monopoly, forgetting that free entry pulls each firm's demand curve in until it just touches ATC.

topics.title: Payoff Matrices and Dominant Strategies
topics.short: A dominant strategy is a player's best choice no matter what the other player does.
topics.trouble: Students compare payoffs across players (my 5 against your 3) instead of comparing one player's own payoffs across that player's choices.

topics.title: Nash Equilibrium and the Prisoner's Dilemma
topics.short: In a Nash equilibrium no player can do better by changing alone, which is why cartels are hard to hold together.
topics.trouble: Students think a Nash equilibrium must be the best outcome for both players. In a prisoner's dilemma it is worse for both than cooperating.

topics.title: Marginal Revenue Product and Hiring
topics.short: Hire workers until the marginal revenue product of the last one equals the wage.
topics.trouble: Students compare the wage with the marginal product in units of output instead of with marginal product times the price (or times marginal revenue).

topics.title: Shifts in Labor Demand and Supply
topics.short: Product prices, productivity and other inputs shift labor demand; population, preferences and pay elsewhere shift labor supply.
topics.trouble: Students shift labor demand when the wage changes, which is a movement along the curve, or forget that labor demand is derived from demand for the product.

topics.title: The Least-Cost Mix of Inputs
topics.short: Use inputs so the last dollar spent on each adds the same output: MPL/w = MPK/r.
topics.trouble: Students hire more of the input with the higher marginal product without dividing by its price.

topics.title: Monopsony
topics.short: A single buyer of labor must raise the wage for everyone to hire one more worker, so it hires fewer workers at a lower wage.
topics.trouble: Students read the wage from the marginal factor cost curve at the hiring point. The wage comes from the labor supply curve.

topics.title: Negative Externalities
topics.short: When a cost spills onto bystanders, the market produces more than the efficient amount.
topics.trouble: Students put the deadweight loss on the wrong side of the efficient quantity, or think the market underproduces goods that pollute.

topics.title: Positive Externalities
topics.short: When a benefit spills onto bystanders, the market produces less than the efficient amount.
topics.trouble: Students draw a benefit from consuming a good (like a flu shot) on the supply side. It puts a marginal social benefit curve above the demand curve.

topics.title: Correcting Externalities
topics.short: A per-unit tax equal to the marginal external cost, a subsidy, tradable permits or direct rules can move output toward the efficient amount.
topics.trouble: Students think the efficient amount of pollution is zero. It is where the marginal benefit of cutting pollution equals the marginal cost of cutting it.

topics.title: Rival and Excludable Goods
topics.short: Private goods, public goods, common resources and club goods differ in whether people can be kept out and whether one person's use leaves less for others.
topics.trouble: Students call anything the government provides a public good. A public school can exclude and is largely rival; national defense is neither.

topics.title: Public Goods and Free Riders
topics.short: Because no one can be kept from using a public good, people can ride free, and markets tend to supply too little.
topics.trouble: Students compare the cost with one person's benefit, instead of with the sum of everyone's benefits, when deciding if a public good is worth providing.

topics.title: Measuring Income Inequality
topics.short: The Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient show how evenly income is shared.
topics.trouble: Students read a Lorenz curve farther from the diagonal as more equal, or think a higher Gini coefficient means a more equal distribution.
